conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported by the strongest directly relevant randomized evidence and meta-analyses, concluding that chlorhexidine-alcohol reduces surgical-site infection compared with iodine-alcohol solutions.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** Your claim is supported by the strongest directly relevant randomized evidence, though the overall effect is better described as a modest reduction rather than a guarantee.

In a randomized trial comparing the exact preparations in your claim, 30-day superficial or deep surgical-site infection occurred in 4.0% with chlorhexidine–alcohol versus 7.3% with iodine–alcohol (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90; *P*=0.02). That is an absolute reduction of 3.3 percentage points—about 1 fewer infection per 30 cesareans prepared with chlorhexidine–alcohol rather than iodine–alcohol.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

Evidence syntheses are consistent: a cesarean-specific systematic review/meta-analysis concluded chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces SSI compared with povidone–iodine solutions, and the Cochrane review judged chlorhexidine gluconate *probably slightly* more effective than povidone iodine (moderate-certainty evidence).  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32580252/

**Important qualification:** Not every trial found a statistically discernible advantage. CAPICA found no lower SSI frequency with chlorhexidine–alcohol compared with an **aqueous** povidone–iodine scrub-and-paint regimen (reported rates about 6.3% vs 7.0%). That comparison differs from iodine–alcohol, so it does not directly overturn the main finding, but it shows outcomes can depend on formulation, technique, and setting.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/
